messages.content: What are the most common chords in a pop song?

function.name: music_theory_primary_triads
function.description: Get the primary triads for a given key signature. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

key_signature.description: The key signature to calculate the primary triads for.

include_inversions.description: Whether or not to include inversions in the returned triads.

message.content:
In contemporary pop music, the harmonic palette tends to stay fairly tight and predictable.  The most frequently used chords are those that belong to the **primary triads** of the key (I, IV, V) plus the relative minor (vi) and the sub‑dominant minor (ii).  These five chords form the backbone of many pop progressions.  

A few of the most iconic patterns that pop songs rely on are:

| Progression | Example in C major | Typical feel |
|-------------|-------------------|--------------|
| I – V – vi – IV | C – G – Am – F | “50s progression” – bright, nostalgic |
| I – vi – IV – V | C – Am – F – G | Classic “doo‑wop” cadence |
| I – IV – V – I | C – F – G – C | Standard verse/chorus turnaround |
| ii – V – I | Dm – G – C | Jazz‑influenced turnarounds that add tension |
| vi – IV – I – V | Am – F – C – G | Modern “pop‑rock” loop |

These chords are chosen because they are diatonic (no accidentals), so they fit naturally into the key and give listeners a sense of resolution.  Because of their ubiquity, pop songs often use them in various combinations, sometimes adding a secondary dominant (e.g., V/V) or a borrowed chord (e.g., bVII) for color, but the core of the progression usually stays within this small set.
